ii. In the Oxidation of Aromatic Side Chains

Alkaline potassium manganate (VII) solution oxidizes any hydrocarbon side chain attached to a benzene ring back to a single –COOH group. Prolonged heating is necessary. For example: as shown in the figure.

In case of the ethyl side chain, carbon dioxide is also produced but in each case, the main product is benzoic acid.

14.3.3.3 Potassium Manganate (VII) as an Oxidizing Agent in Titrations

KMnO₄ is a strong oxidizing agent with intense dark purple colour. During reduction, the purple permanganate ion changes into colourless Mn²⁺ ion.

Potassium manganate (VII) solution is used to find the concentration of all sorts of reducing agents. It is always used in acidic solution.

For example, it oxidizes

Iron(II) ions to iron(III) ions

Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻ (acidic)

Hydrogen peroxide solution to oxygen

H₂O₂ → O₂ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻

Sulphite ions (IV) to sulphate ions (VI) ions

SO₃²⁻ + H₂O → SO₄²⁻ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻

In each case, the half-equation for the manganate (VII) ions in acidic solution is:

MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O

14.3.4 Iron

Iron is the second most abundant metal in the Earth’s crust. Concentrated deposits of iron ore are found in many localities, thus making it easy to mine. Iron is a transition metal with a symbol “Fe” and atomic number 26 and its atomic mass is 55.845 a.m.u.

14.3.4.1 Oxidation States

Most common oxidation states of iron are +2 and +3 but it can also exists in the form of Fe⁴⁺, Fe⁵⁺ and Fe⁶⁺. The +6 oxidation state of Fe is very rare. The Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ oxidation states are stable states.

Iron in the +2 oxidation state is known as the ferrous ion. This ion is pale green in colour and is very easily oxidized to ferric ion. Even traces of dissolved oxygen in solution will complete this oxidation. Solution of ferrous ion is sometimes used as reducing agent.

Most solutions containing ferric ions are usually yellow or yellow–brown due to formation of [Fe(H₂O)₅(OH)]²⁺. Fe³⁺(aq) yields a dark blue precipitate called Prussian blue, Fe₄[Fe(CN)₆]₃ is formed, when treated with potassium ferrocyanide, K₄[Fe(CN)₆](aq).

14.3.4.2 Iron as Catalyst in Haber’s Process

In the Haber process, hydrogen reacts with nitrogen to produce ammonia. Without catalyst, the process would proceed too slowly to be economically viable. The reaction takes place according to the following steps:

N₂ + H₂ → N₂H₂

N₂H₂ + H₂ → N₂H₄

14.3.3.3 Potassium Manganate (VII) as an Oxidizing Agent in Titrations

KMnO₄ is a strong oxidizing agent with intense dark purple colour. During reduction, the purple permanganate ion changes into colourless Mn²⁺ ion.

Potassium manganate (VII) solution is used to find the concentration of all sorts of reducing agents. It is always used in acidic solution.

For example, it oxidizes

Iron(II) ions to iron(III) ions

Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻ (acidic)

Hydrogen peroxide solution to oxygen

H₂O₂ → O₂ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻

Sulphite ions (IV) to sulphate ions (VI) ions

SO₃²⁻ + H₂O → SO₄²⁻ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻

In each case, the half-equation for the manganate (VII) ions in acidic solution is:

MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O

14.3.4 Iron

Iron is the second most abundant metal in the Earth’s crust. Concentrated deposits of iron ore are found in many localities, thus making it easy to mine. Iron is a transition metal with a symbol “Fe” and atomic number 26 and its atomic mass is 55.845 a.m.u.

14.3.4.1 Oxidation States

Most common oxidation states of iron are +2 and +3 but it can also exists in the form of Fe⁴⁺, Fe⁵⁺ and Fe⁶⁺. The +6 oxidation state of Fe is very rare. The Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ oxidation states are stable states.

Iron in the +2 oxidation state is known as the ferrous ion. This ion is pale green in colour and is very easily oxidized to ferric ion. Even traces of dissolved oxygen in solution will complete this oxidation. Solution of ferrous ion is sometimes used as reducing agent.

Most solutions containing ferric ions are usually yellow or yellow–brown due to formation of [Fe(H₂O)₅(OH)]²⁺. Fe³⁺(aq) yields a dark blue precipitate called Prussian blue, Fe₄[Fe(CN)₆]₃ is formed, when treated with potassium ferrocyanide, K₄[Fe(CN)₆](aq).

14.3.4.2 Iron as Catalyst in Haber’s Process

In the Haber process, hydrogen reacts with nitrogen to produce ammonia. Without catalyst, the process would proceed too slowly to be economically viable. The reaction takes place according to the following steps:
